growth_story.headline: Uruguay's income per person surged in the commodity boom after the 2002 crisis, but has grown only 1.3 percent a year since 2014.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Uruguay grew 3.7 percent a year in 1990–1997, a time the IMF calls rapid growth. In 1998–2005 growth averaged just 0.1 percent a year: crises in Brazil and Argentina, its main trading partners, pushed it into recession, and in 2002 a run on the banks that began with Argentine depositors became the country's most severe financial crisis, with income per person falling 7.9 percent that year. Growth then ran at 5.2 percent a year in 2006–2013, as commodity prices boomed, investment rose and economic management improved after the crisis. Since 2014 growth has averaged 1.3 percent a year, as export prices and growth in trading partners fell and productivity stalled, and the pandemic (a fall of 7.4 percent in 2020) and a severe drought in 2023 added fresh shocks. Even so, income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025.

threads.title: Contagion from Argentina, 2002
threads.text: Brazil and Argentina were Uruguay's main trading partners, so their crises dragged it into a long recession from 1999. In 2002 Argentine savers pulled money out of Uruguayan banks, and the run spread through a banking system that relied heavily on dollars.

citations.title: Uruguay: Ex Post Assessment of Longer-Term Program Engagement—Staff Report; Public Information Notice on the Executive Board Discussion; and Statement by the Executive Director for Uruguay (IMF Country Report No. 05/202)
citations.quote: The crisis was triggered by deposit withdrawals from cash-strapped Argentine residents and soon developed into a more generalized run on the banks.

citations.title: Uruguay: Ex Post Assessment of Longer-Term Program Engagement—Staff Report; Public Information Notice on the Executive Board Discussion; and Statement by the Executive Director for Uruguay (IMF Country Report No. 05/202)
citations.quote: These included crises in Brazil and Argentina—Uruguay’s main trading partners, jointly accounting for almost one half of Uruguay’s exports in the mid-1990s

citations.title: Uruguay: Ex Post Assessment of Longer-Term Program Engagement—Staff Report; Public Information Notice on the Executive Board Discussion; and Statement by the Executive Director for Uruguay (IMF Country Report No. 05/202)
citations.quote: the crisis was made possible and more damaging by long standing vulnerabilities in the banking system—dollarization but also insufficient prudential regulation

threads.title: The commodity boom and its end
threads.text: After the crisis, a boom in commodity prices, good conditions abroad and a wave of investment lifted growth. By 2012–13 export prices and growth in the main trading partners had started to fall, and growth later slowed with them.

citations.title: Uruguay Systematic Country Diagnostic Update
citations.quote: In line with the region, the end of the commodity price boom ushered in a period of lower growth rates and less poverty reduction

citations.title: Uruguay Systematic Country Diagnostic Update
citations.quote: Export prices and economic growth among main trading partners had already started to decline by 2012–13.

citations.title: Uruguay Systematic Country Diagnostic Update
citations.quote: The share of investment over GDP nearly doubled, from 12 percent in 2002 to a high of 22 percent in 2012.

threads.title: Weather and a narrow export base
threads.text: Uruguay's exports rest on a fairly narrow set of commodities, so rain and world prices move growth. In 2023, a year of severe drought, income per person grew 0.8 percent; it rebounded to 3.4 percent in 2024 on a surge in farm exports.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Uruguay
citations.quote: Uruguay remains exposed to external and climate-related shocks, largely due to its relatively narrow commodity export base, reliance on imported fuels and production inputs

citations.title: Uruguay: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Uruguay (IMF Country Report No. 25/287)
citations.quote: After a severe drought in 2023, Uruguay’s economy rebounded strongly in 2024 driven by a surge in agricultural exports.

threads.title: A shrinking, aging population
threads.text: Uruguay's population stopped growing around 2020 and is getting older. The IMF sees this aging as a risk to growth.

citations.title: Uruguay: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Uruguay (IMF Country Report No. 25/287)
citations.quote: Uruguay’s population peaked at 3.5 million in 2020 and is expected to decline steadily to 3.0 million in 2070 alongside population aging.

citations.title: Uruguay: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Uruguay (IMF Country Report No. 25/287)
citations.quote: Population aging poses risks to growth and sustainability

threads.title: A new government in 2025
threads.text: A new government took office in March 2025. It has set out plans to raise private investment while keeping the economy stable and widening social protection.

citations.title: Uruguay: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Uruguay (IMF Country Report No. 25/287)
citations.quote: A new administration led by president Yamandú Orsi took office in March 2025, marking the return of the Frente Amplio coalition to power.

citations.title: Uruguay: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Uruguay (IMF Country Report No. 25/287)
citations.quote: The new administration’s agenda seeks to balance inclusive growth with macroeconomic stability, boosting private investment and strengthening social protection.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 1.8 percent in 2025, down from 3.4 percent in 2024. The World Bank's October 2026 note expects growth to slow again in 2026. Last summer's drought cut soybean yields, and in the second quarter weaker net exports outweighed strong spending at home.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Uruguay
citations.quote: Real GDP growth is expected to moderate to 1.2 percent in 2026, reflecting external headwinds and reduced soybean yields

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Uruguay
citations.quote: Strong domestic demand was outweighed by weaker net exports.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a decade of weak growth in total output. Income per person did a little better, at 1.3 percent a year over 2016–2025, and reached its highest level yet in 2025, because the population has stopped growing. The sources also date the start of the turn to 2012–13, when export prices and growth in trading partners began to fall, while the data put the break in 2014.
